title: Inferential Statistics and the t-Test
summary: Inferential statistics draws conclusions about a whole population from a sample. This chapter covers population and sample, parameter and statistic, hypothesis testing, and the t-test for one sample and for two independent small samples.

notes.heading: Population, sample, parameter and statistic
notes.html:
• Population: the complete set of items under study (size N). Sample: a part of the population chosen to represent it (size n).
  • Parameter: a numerical measure of the population, e.g. population mean μ and standard deviation σ. It is fixed but usually unknown.
  • Statistic: a numerical measure computed from a sample, e.g. sample mean x̄ and sample standard deviation s. It changes from sample to sample.
  • Statistical inference: using a statistic to estimate or test a claim about a parameter.
  • A sample should be representative and chosen at random (simple random sampling, systematic, stratified) so that every unit has a fair chance of selection.

notes.heading: Sampling distribution and standard error
notes.html:
If we take all possible samples of size n and compute x̄ for each, the values of x̄ form the sampling distribution of the mean.

  • Mean of the sampling distribution = μ.
  • Its standard deviation is called the standard error: SE = σ/√n (or s/√n when σ is unknown).
  • Central Limit Theorem: for large n (n ≥ 30) the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal whatever the shape of the population.
  • For small samples (n < 30) from a normal population with σ unknown, we use the t-distribution.

notes.heading: Hypothesis testing: the vocabulary
notes.html:
• Null hypothesis H0: the statement of no difference, e.g. μ = μ0. It is assumed true until evidence says otherwise.
  • Alternative hypothesis H1: what we accept if H0 is rejected: μ ≠ μ0 (two-tailed), μ > μ0 or μ < μ0 (one-tailed).
  • Level of significance α: the probability of rejecting a true H0; usually 5% (0.05) or 1%.
  • Critical region: the set of values of the test statistic for which H0 is rejected.
  • Degrees of freedom (df): number of independent observations = n − 1 for one sample.
  • Type I error: rejecting a true H0. Type II error: accepting a false H0.

Decision rule: if |t calculated| > t tabulated, reject H0; otherwise do not reject H0.

notes.heading: The t-distribution
notes.html:
• Bell-shaped and symmetric about 0, like the normal curve, but flatter with thicker tails.
  • Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom; as df increases it approaches the standard normal curve.
  • Used when the sample is small (n < 30), the population is normal and σ is unknown.

notes.heading: One-sample t-test with worked examples
notes.html:
t = (x̄ − μ0) / (s/√n), df = n − 1, where s = √[Σ(x − x̄)2/(n − 1)].

Example 1

A sample of 9 packets has mean weight 52 g and s = 6 g. Test at 5% whether the population mean is 48 g.

H0: μ = 48; H1: μ ≠ 48. t = (52 − 48)/(6/√9) = 4/2 = 2. df = 8, t0.05 = 2.306. Since 2 < 2.306, H0 is not rejected: the mean may be taken as 48 g.

Example 2 (raw data)

Sample: 10, 12, 9, 11, 13. Test μ = 9 at 5%.

x̄ = 55/5 = 11. Deviations: −1, 1, −2, 0, 2; Σ(x − x̄)2 = 10. s2 = 10/4 = 2.5, s = 1.581.

t = (11 − 9)/(1.581/√5) = 2/0.7071 = 2.83. df = 4, t0.05 = 2.776. Since 2.83 > 2.776, reject H0: the mean differs significantly from 9.

notes.heading: Two independent samples t-test
notes.html:
Used to test whether two small independent samples come from populations with the same mean (equal variances assumed).

t = (x̄1 − x̄2) / [S √(1/n1 + 1/n2)], df = n1 + n2 − 2

Pooled variance: S2 = [(n1 − 1)s12 + (n2 − 1)s22] / (n1 + n2 − 2)

Example 3

Group A: n1 = 10, x̄1 = 75, s12 = 16. Group B: n2 = 12, x̄2 = 70, s22 = 25. Test at 5%.

H0: μ1 = μ2. S2 = (9 × 16 + 11 × 25)/20 = 419/20 = 20.95, S = 4.577.

√(1/10 + 1/12) = √0.1833 = 0.4282. t = 5/(4.577 × 0.4282) = 5/1.960 = 2.55.

df = 20, t0.05 = 2.086. Since 2.55 > 2.086, reject H0: the two means differ significantly.

notes.heading: Common mistakes
notes.html:
• Dividing by n instead of n − 1 when computing s from raw data.
  • Using df = n instead of n − 1 (or n1 + n2 instead of n1 + n2 − 2).
  • Writing 'H0 is accepted/proved'. Write 'H0 is not rejected'.
  • Forgetting to state H0, H1 and the conclusion in words: each carries marks.
  • Comparing t with the table value without taking the absolute value.

questions.q: Distinguish between a parameter and a statistic.
questions.answerHtml: A parameter is a measure of the population (e.g. μ) and is fixed; a statistic is a measure of a sample (e.g. x̄) and varies from sample to sample.

questions.q: Define null hypothesis and level of significance.
questions.answerHtml:
Null hypothesis (H0) is the statement of no difference that is tested, e.g. μ = μ0.

Level of significance (α) is the maximum probability of rejecting H0 when it is true, usually taken as 5% or 1%.

questions.q: A machine is set to fill 500 ml bottles. A sample of 16 bottles has mean 496 ml and s = 8 ml. Is the machine working properly at 5% level? (t<sub>0.05</sub> for 15 df = 2.131)
questions.answerHtml:
H0: μ = 500; H1: μ ≠ 500.

t = (496 − 500)/(8/√16) = −4/2 = −2, so |t| = 2.

df = 15, table value 2.131. Since 2 < 2.131, H0 is not rejected. The machine may be regarded as working properly.

questions.q: Ten students scored: 70, 72, 68, 75, 71, 69, 74, 73, 70, 68 after a coaching course. Test whether the mean score is 68 at 5% level. (t<sub>0.05</sub> for 9 df = 2.262)

Two brands of bulbs were tested. Brand X: n = 8, mean life 1,200 h, s<sup>2</sup> = 900. Brand Y: n = 7, mean life 1,150 h, s<sup>2</sup> = 1,600. Is the difference in mean life significant at 5%? (t<sub>0.05</sub> for 13 df = 2.160)
questions.answerHtml:
H0: μX = μY; H1: μX ≠ μY.

S2 = (7 × 900 + 6 × 1600)/13 = (6300 + 9600)/13 = 1223.08, so S = 34.97.

√(1/8 + 1/7) = √0.2679 = 0.5175.

t = (1200 − 1150)/(34.97 × 0.5175) = 50/18.10 = 2.76.

df = 8 + 7 − 2 = 13, table value 2.160. Since 2.76 > 2.160, reject H0.

Conclusion: the mean lives of the two brands differ significantly; Brand X lasts longer.
